content.content:
1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
64

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
52

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	## The library order
74	
75	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76	
77	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78	
79	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81	
82	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
86	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
87	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
90	
91	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
92	
93	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
94	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
95	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
96	
97	## Name resolution
98	
99	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
100	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
101	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
102	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
103	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
104	
105	## Building
106	
107	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
108	
109	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
110	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
111	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
113	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
114	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
115	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
116	
117	## After an edit of the library
118	
119	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
120	
121	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
122	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
123	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
124	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
125	
126	## Symptoms of a skipped step
127	
128	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
129	
130	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
131	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
132	
133	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
134	
135	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
136	
137	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
138	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
139	
140	Two more facts help you read a run:
141	
142	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
143	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
144

1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
2	
3	**prompt cache**
4	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
5	
6	**interrupt**
7	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
8	
9	**stop of the process**
10	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
11	
12	**automatic permission check**
13	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
14	
15	## The Bash tool and waits
16	
17	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
18	
19	- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
20	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
21	
22	## Long commands
23	
24	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
25	
26	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
27	
28	Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.
29	
30	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
31	
32	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
33	
34	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
35	
36	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
37	        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
38	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
39	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
40	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
41	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
42	        done
43	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
44	    }
45	
46	If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.
47	
48	- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
49	- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.
50	
51	## Stopping processes
52	
53	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
54	
55	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
56	
57	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
58	
59	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
60	
61	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
62	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
63	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
64	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
65	
66	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
67	
68	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
69	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
70

12	\chapter{Overview}
13	\chaplabel{overview}
14	
15	\note{Keyword and varargs parameters,
16	array comprehensions,
17	dimensions and units,
18	tests and properties,
19	distributions,
20	some ASCII conversion, and
21	some common types are not yet supported.
22	
23	Some examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter.}
24	
25	In this chapter, we provide a high-level overview of the entire Fortress
26	language. We present most features in this chapter through the use of examples,
27	which should be accessible to programmers of other languages.
28	In this chapter, unlike the rest of the specification,
29	no attempt is made to provide complete descriptions
30	of the various language features presented. Instead, we intend this overview to
31	provide useful context for reading other sections of this specification,
32	which provide rigorous definitions for what is merely
33	introduced here.
34	
35	\section{The Fortress Programming Environment}
36	\seclabel{programming-env}
37	
38	\revision{revival-environment}{\secref{programming-env} to \secref{apitool}
39	are rewritten to describe how a program is run with the implementation in
40	the revival's repository.
41	Every command is printed as it runs there, with the output that it gave.
42	The Working Draft's text of these sections, which describes a store of
43	components that was not built, is kept in \secref{revival-environment}.}
44	
45	This section and the two after it show how a Fortress program is written, and
46	how it is run with the implementation in the revival's repository
47	(\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
48	Each command is printed as it is typed into a shell, in the folder that holds
49	the files of the examples.
50	The files of the examples are printed as they are typed, in ASCII;
51	the section on rendering below shows how such code is rendered.
52	
53	A Fortress program is a \emph{component}, stored in a source file.
54	The following component is the program of this section:
55	
56	\begin{verbatim}
57	component HelloWorld
58	export Executable
59	
60	run(): () = println "Hello, world!"
61	
62	end
63	\end{verbatim}
64	
65	The first line names the component.
66	The second line is an \emph{export statement}, which \secref{overview:apis}
67	explains.
68	The fourth line defines a function \VAR{run}, which takes no parameter,
69	returns no value, and prints one line.
70	A program starts with a call of its function \VAR{run}.
71	
72	A source file must contain exactly one component declaration, and its name
73	must match the file name without the file extension \shellcommand{.fss}.
74	So this component is stored in a file named \shellcommand{HelloWorld.fss}.
75	If the two names differ, the implementation refuses the file with this
76	message:
77	
78	\begin{verbatim}
79	Component/API names must match their enclosing file names.
80	\end{verbatim}
81	
82	A program is run in one of two ways: under the interpreter, or compiled.
83	
84	The commands of this chapter assume an installed implementation, with the
85	command \shellcommand{fortress} on the shell's path; the file
86	\shellcommand{README.md} of the repository says how to build one.
87	
88	\subsection{Running a Program under the Interpreter}
89	
90	The interpreter reads a source file and runs it:
91	
92	\begin{verbatim}
93	fortress HelloWorld.fss
94	\end{verbatim}
95	
96	The command prints:
97	
98	\begin{verbatim}
99	Hello, world!
100	\end{verbatim}
101	
102	The command \shellcommand{fortress walk HelloWorld.fss} is the same command.
103	The interpreter does not check the static types of a program.
104	A type error stops the program when the run reaches it.
105	
106	\subsection{Compiling and Running a Program}
107	
108	The compiler checks the static types of a component and writes bytecode of
109	the Java Virtual Machine for it.
110	The program is compiled and run with two commands:
111	
112	\begin{verbatim}
113	fortress compile HelloWorld.fss
114	fortress run HelloWorld
115	\end{verbatim}
116	
117	The first command prints nothing.
118	The second prints:
119	
120	\begin{verbatim}
121	Hello, world!
122	\end{verbatim}
123	
124	The command \shellcommand{fortress compile} takes a source file.
125	It prints nothing when it succeeds, and a static error stops it with a message.
126	The command \shellcommand{fortress run} takes the name of a component, not a
127	file.
128	It runs the bytecode that the last compilation of that component wrote, and
129	compiles nothing.
130	After a change of a source file, the interpreter runs the changed program, and
131	\shellcommand{fortress run} runs the old one until the file is compiled again.
132	
133	\label{overviewComponent}
134	\section{Exports and Imports}
135	\seclabel{overview:apis}
136	
137	When a component is defined, it can include \emph{export statements}.
138	For example, the component \TYP{HelloWorld} includes the export statement
139	``\EXP{\KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}}''.
140	Export statements list various \emph{APIs}
141	that a component implements.
142	Unlike in other languages, APIs in
143	Fortress are themselves program constructs; programmers can rely on
144	standard APIs, and declare new ones. API declarations are sequences of
145	declarations of
146	variables, functions, and other program constructs, along with their
147	types and other
148	supporting declarations. For example, here is the definition of API
149	\TYP{Executable}, which the library provides:
150	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Executable.tex}
151	
152	This API contains the declaration of a single function \VAR{run},
153	which takes no argument.
154	The return type of \VAR{run} is \EXP{()}, pronounced ``void''.
155	Type \EXP{()} may be used in Fortress as a return type
156	for functions that have no meaningful return value.
157	There is a single value with type \EXP{()}:
158	the value \EXP{()}, also pronounced ``void''.
159	References to value \EXP{()} as opposed
160	to type \EXP{()} are resolved by context.
161	
162	A component that exports an API must provide a definition
163	for every program construct declared in the API.
164	For example, because the component \TYP{HelloWorld} exports the API
165	\TYP{Executable}, it must include a definition for the function \VAR{run}.
166	The compiler checks this.
167	The interpreter does not.
168	
169	An API is defined in a file with the file extension \shellcommand{.fsi}.
170	As a component's file, the file holds exactly one API, and the name of the API
171	must match the file name without the file extension.
172	For example, the following API is written to a file named
173	\shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi}:
174	
175	\begin{verbatim}
176	api Zeepf
177	
178	foo(s: String): ()
179	baz(s: String): String
180	
181	end
182	\end{verbatim}
183	
184	The following component implements this API.
185	The implementation finds the component that implements an API only under the
186	name of the API, so the component is named \TYP{Zeepf} too, and is written to
187	a file named \shellcommand{Zeepf.fss}.
188	Components and APIs exist in separate namespaces, and therefore
189	it is allowed for a component to have the same name as an API.
190	
191	\begin{verbatim}
192	component Zeepf
193	export Zeepf
194	
195	foo(s: String): () = println("foo says: " || s)
196	baz(s: String): String = s || "!"
197	
198	end
199	\end{verbatim}
200	
201	Components are also allowed to \emph{import} APIs. A component that
202	imports an API is allowed to use any of the program constructs
203	declared in that API. For example, the following component, written to a file
204	named \shellcommand{Blargh.fss}, imports the API
205	\TYP{Zeepf} and calls the functions \VAR{foo} and \VAR{baz} declared in
206	\TYP{Zeepf}:
207	
208	\begin{verbatim}
209	component Blargh
210	import Zeepf.{ foo, baz }
211	export Executable
212	
213	run(): () = foo(baz("whatever"))
214	
215	end
216	\end{verbatim}
217	
218	In an import statement of the form:
219	%import A.{S}
220	\begin{Fortress}
221	\(\KWD{import}\:A.\{S\}\)
222	\end{Fortress}
223	all names in the list of names \VAR{S} are imported from API $A$, and can be
224	referred to as unqualified names within the importing component.
225	
226	Note that no component refers directly to another component,
227	or to constructs defined in another component.
228	Instead, \emph{all external references go through APIs}.
229	This level of indirection provides a way to hide implementation details in a
230	component.
231	
232	The interpreter runs the component \TYP{Blargh} as it runs any program.
233	It finds the files of the API \TYP{Zeepf} and of the component \TYP{Zeepf} in
234	the same folder:
235	
236	\begin{verbatim}
237	fortress Blargh.fss
238	\end{verbatim}
239	
240	The command prints:
241	
242	\begin{verbatim}
243	foo says: whatever!
244	\end{verbatim}
245	
246	To run the compiled program, the component is \emph{linked}.
247	The command \shellcommand{fortress link} compiles a component and the
248	components that implement the APIs that it imports, and joins them.
249	It prints nothing when it succeeds.
250	
251	\begin{verbatim}
252	fortress link Blargh.fss
253	fortress run Blargh
254	\end{verbatim}
255	
256	The second command prints:
257	
258	\begin{verbatim}
259	foo says: whatever!
260	\end{verbatim}
261	
262	\section{Automatic Generation of APIs}
263	\seclabel{apitool}
264	
265	The command \shellcommand{fortress api} generates an API from a component:
266	
267	\begin{verbatim}
268	fortress api Zeepf.fss
269	\end{verbatim}
270	
271	The command prints the API:
272	
273	\begin{verbatim}
274	api Zeepf
275	
276	foo(s: String): ()
277	
278	baz(s: String): String
279	
280	end
281	\end{verbatim}
282	
283	The API has the name of the component.
284	It declares every top-level definition of the component that does not include
285	the modifier \KWD{private}.
286	
287	With the option \shellcommand{-out}, the command writes the API to a file:
288	
289	\begin{verbatim}

291	\end{verbatim}
292	
293	The command prints:
294

297	\end{verbatim}

300	Here it replaces the file \shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi} that was written by hand

418	\subsection{Juxtaposition and function application}
419	
420	In the definition of \VAR{factorial},
421	note the juxtaposition of parameter \VAR{n} with the recursive
422	call \EXP{\VAR{factorial}(n - 1)}.
423	In Fortress, as in mathematics,
424	multiplication is represented through juxtaposition.
425	By default,
426	two expressions of numeric type that are juxtaposed
427	represent a multiplication.
428	On the other hand,
429	juxtaposition of an expression of function type
430	with another expression to its right
431	represents function application,
432	as in the following example:
433	
434	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.sin.tex}
435	
436	Moreover, juxtaposition of expressions of string type
437	represents concatenation, as in the following example:
438	
439	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.String.tex}
440	
441	In fact, juxtaposition is an operator in Fortress,
442	just like \EXP{+} and \EXP{-},
443	that is overloaded based on the runtime types of its arguments.
444	
445	There is a special case concerning juxtaposition that is important to mention:
446	When writing a numeric literal, the \emph{digit-group separator},
447	\txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE} (U+202F),
448	may be included between the digits in order to improve readability.
449	In ASCII,
450	this character can be abbreviated in the context of a numeric literal
451	(\emph{and only in this context}) with the character \txt{'}.
452	For example, the number 299,792,458 can be denoted in ASCII by the
453	following numeric literal:
454	
455	\begin{verbatim}
456	299'792'458
457	\end{verbatim}
458	
459	This literal is converted into Unicode by replacing all occurrences of
460	\txt{'} with \txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE}:
461	%299 792 458
462	\begin{Fortress}
463	\(299{}\;792{}\;458\)
464	\end{Fortress}
465	This is not an application of the juxtaposition operator;
466	rather, it is a single token.
467	Note that commas cannot be used to separate digits because ambiguities
468	would arise with the use of commas in other expressions,
469	such as tuples.

471	\subsection{Keyword Parameters}
472	
473	Functions in Fortress can be defined to take keyword arguments by
474	providing default values for parameters. In
475	the following example:
476	
477	%makeColor(red:ZZ64 = 0, green:ZZ64 = 0, blue:ZZ64 = 0) =
478	%   if 0 <= red <= 255 AND 0 <= green <= 255 AND 0 <= blue <= 255
479	%   then Color(red,green,blue)
480	%   else throw Error end
481	\begin{Fortress}
482	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{red}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{green}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{blue}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0) =\)\\
483	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{if} 0 \leq \VAR{red} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{green} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{blue} \leq 255 \)\\
484	\(   \KWD{then} \TYP{Color}(\VAR{red},\VAR{green},\VAR{blue})\)\\
485	\(   \KWD{else}\;\;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error} \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
486	\end{Fortress}
487	
488	the function \VAR{makeColor} takes three keyword arguments, all of
489	which default to \EXP{0}. If we call it as follows:
490	
491	%makeColor(green = 255)
492	\begin{Fortress}
493	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{green} = 255)\)
494	\end{Fortress}
495	
496	the arguments \VAR{red} and \VAR{blue} are both given the value \EXP{0}.
497	
498	There are some other aspects of this example worth mentioning.
499	For example,
500	the body of this function consists of an \KWD{if} expression.
501	The test of the \KWD{if} expression checks that
502	all three parameters have values between \EXP{0} and \EXP{255}. The
503	boolean operator \EXP{\leq} is \emph{chained}: An expression of
504	the form \EXP{x \leq y \leq z} is equivalent to the expression
505	\EXP{x \leq y \wedge y \leq z}, just as in mathematical notation.
506	The \KWD{then} clause provides an example of a constructor call in Fortress,
507	and the \KWD{else} clause shows us an example
508	of a \KWD{throw} expression in Fortress.
509	\note{How can we tell this from the example?
510	Indeed, in general, we can't distinguish constructors from other functions
511	looking only at the call sites.}

629	\section{Dimensions and Units}
630	
631	Numeric types in Fortress can be annotated with physical units and
632	dimensions. For example, the following function declares that its
633	parameter is a tuple represented in the units \EXP{\mathrm{kg}} and
634	\EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}},
635	respectively:
636	
637	\note{I MANUALLY EDITED THIS CODE -Victor}
638	%kineticEnergy(m:RR64 kg_, v:RR64 m_/s_):RR64 kg_ m_^2/s_^2 = (m v^2) / 2
639	\begin{Fortress}
640	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(m\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}, v\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}^{2} = (m\ v^{2}) / 2\)
641	\end{Fortress}
642	
643	A value of type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}} is a
644	64-bit float representing a measurement in kilograms.
645	When the function \VAR{kineticEnergy} is called, two values in its tuple
646	argument are statically checked to ensure that they are in the right units.
647	
648	All commonly used dimensions and units are provided in \library.
649	Unit symbols are encoded with trailing underscores;
650	such identifiers are rendered in roman font.
651	For example the unit \EXP{\mathrm{m}} is represented as \verb$m_$.
652	For each unit, both longhand and shorthand names are provided
653	(e.g., \EXP{\mathrm{m}},
654	\EXP{\mathrm{meter}}, and \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}).
655	The various names of a given unit can be used interchangeably.
656	Also, some units (and dimensions) are defined to be synonymous
657	with algebraic combinations of other units (and dimensions).
658	For example, the unit \EXP{\mathrm{N}} is defined to be synonymous
659	with the unit \EXP{\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}}
660	and the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Force}} is defined to be synonymous with
661	\EXP{\mathrm{Mass}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{Acceleration}}.
662	Likewise, the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Acceleration}}
663	is defined to be synonymous with \EXP{\mathrm{Velocity}/\mathrm{Time}}.
664	
665	Measurements in the same unit can be compared, added, subtracted,
666	multiplied and divided.
667	Measurements in different units can be multiplied and divided.
668	For example, we can write the following variable declaration:
669	
670	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5 seconds_
671	\begin{Fortress}
672	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
673	\end{Fortress}
674	
675	However, the following variable declaration is a static error:
676	
677	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 seconds_) / 5 seconds_
678	%I CREATED THE CODE BELOW MANUALLY -Victor
679	\begin{Fortress}
680	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{seconds}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
681	\end{Fortress}
682	
683	In addition, the following variable declaration is a static error
684	because the unit of the left hand side of this declaration
685	is \EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}}
686	whereas the unit of the right hand side
687	is simply \EXP{\mathrm{m}} (or \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}):
688	
689	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5
690	\begin{Fortress}
691	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\)
692	\end{Fortress}
693	
694	It is also possible to convert a measurement in one unit to
695	a measurement of another unit of the same dimension,
696	as in the following example:
697	
698	%kineticEnergy(3.14 kg_, 32 f_/s_ in m_/s_)
699	\begin{Fortress}
700	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(3.14\,\mathrm{kg}, 32\,\mathrm{f}/\mathrm{s} \KWD{in} \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\)
701	\end{Fortress}
702	
703	The second argument to \EXP{\VAR{kineticEnergy} } is a measurement in
704	feet per second,
705	converted to meters per second.

713	collection as an \emph{aggregate expression}.
714	The elements of an aggregate expression are computed in parallel.

769	\section{Comprehensions}
770	Another way in which Fortress mimics mathematical notation is in its support for
771	\emph{comprehensions}.  Comprehensions describe the elements of a collection by
772	providing a rule that holds for all of the collection's elements.  The elements
773	of the collection are computed in parallel by default.
774	For example, we define a set \VAR{s} that consists of all elements of another
775	set \VAR{t} divided by 2, as follows:
776	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.s.tex}
777	
778	The expression to the left of the vertical bar
779	explains that elements of \VAR{s} consist of every value \EXP{x/2}
780	for every valid value of \VAR{x} (determined by the right hand side).
781	The expression to the right of the vertical bar
782	explains how the elements \VAR{x} are to be \emph{generated}
783	(in this case, from the set \VAR{t}).
784	The right hand side of a comprehension can consist of multiple generators.
785	For example, the following set consists of every element
786	resulting from the sum of an element of \VAR{s} with an element of \VAR{t}:
787	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.sum.tex}
788	
789	The right hand side of a comprehension can also contain
790	\emph{filtering expressions} to constrain the elements provided by other clauses.
791	For example, we can stipulate that \VAR{v} consists of
792	all nonnegative elements of \VAR{t} as follows:
793	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.filter.tex}
794	
795	There is a comprehension expression for every form of aggregate expression.
796	For example, here is a list comprehension in Fortress:
797	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.l.tex}
798	The elements of this list consist of
799	all elements of the set \VAR{v} multiplied by \EXP{2}.
800	
801	In the case of an array comprehension, the expression to the left of the bar
802	includes a tuple indexing the elements of the array.
803	For example, the following comprehension describes a \EXP{3 \times 3}
804	array, all of whose elements are zero.
805	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- {0,1,2}, y <- {0,1,2}]
806	\begin{Fortress}
807	\([(x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}, y \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}]\)
808	\end{Fortress}
809	
810	The collection of elements \EXP{0} through \EXP{2} can also be expressed via a range expression, as follows:
811	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- 0:2, y <- 0:2]
812	\begin{Fortress}
813	\([(x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2, y \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2]\)
814	\end{Fortress}
815	
816	An array comprehension can consist of multiple clauses. The clauses are run in the order provided,
817	with declarations from later clauses shadowing declarations from earlier clauses. For example, the following
818	comprehension describes a \EXP{3 \times 3} identity matrix:
819	
820	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- 0:2, y <- 0:2
821	% (x,x) = 1 | x <- 0:2]
822	\begin{Fortress}
823	\(\ [ \)\pushtabs\=\+\((x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2, y \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2\)\\
824	\( (x,x) = 1 \mid x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}2]\)\-\\\poptabs
825	\end{Fortress}

829	\section{Summations and Products}
830	As with mathematical notation, Fortress provides syntactic support for
831	summations and productions (and other big operations) over the elements of a collection.
832	For example, an alternative definition of \VAR{factorial} is as follows:
833	
834	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.big.tex}
835	
836	This function definition can be written in ASCII as follows:
837	
838	\begin{verbatim}
839	factorial(n) = PROD[i <- 1:n] i
840	\end{verbatim}
841	
842	The character \EXP{\prod} is written \txt{PROD}.  Likewise,
843	\EXP{\sum} is written \txt{SUM}.
844	As with comprehensions, the values in the iteration are generated from specified collections.

846	\label{overviewTest}
847	\section{Tests and Properties}
848	Fortress includes support for automated program testing.
849	A new test in a component can be defined using the \KWD{test} modifier
850	on a top-level function definition with type ``\EXP{()\rightarrow()}''.
851	For example, here is a test function that calls the \VAR{factorial}
852	function on some representative values
853	and checks that the calls result in values greater than or equal to what was provided:
854	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Tests.tex}
855	
856	%test factorialResultLarger [x <- 0:100] = x <= factorial(x)
857	\begin{Fortress}
858	\(\KWD{test} \VAR{factorialResultLarger} [x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}100] = x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x)\)
859	\end{Fortress}
860	
861	The values for \VAR{x} are generated from the provided range
862	\EXP{0\COLONOP{}100}.
863	
864	Programs are also allowed to include \emph{property} declarations, documenting boolean conditions that a program is
865	expected to obey. Property declarations are similar syntactically to test declarations. Unlike test declarations,
866	property declarations do not specify explicit finite collections over which the property is expected to hold.
867	Instead, the parameters in a property declaration are declared to have types, and the property is expected to hold
868	over all values of those types. For example, here is a property declaring that \VAR{factorial} is greater than or equal
869	to every argument of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}:
870	
871	%property factorialResultAlwaysLarger = FORALL (x : ZZ) (x <= factorial(x))
872	\begin{Fortress}
873	\(\KWD{property} \VAR{factorialResultAlwaysLarger} = \forall (x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\; (x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x))\)
874	\end{Fortress}
875	
876	When a property declaration includes a name, the property identifier is bound to a function whose parameter and body are that of the property,
877	and whose return type is \TYP{Boolean}.
878	A function bound in this manner is referred to as a \emph{property function}.
879	A property function can be called from within tests to ensure that a
880	property holds at least for all values in some finite set of values.

882	\section{Objects and Traits}
883	\seclabel{overview-objects-traits}
884	
885	A great deal of programming can be done simply through the use of
886	functions, top-level
887	variables, and standard types. However, Fortress also includes a trait and object system for
888	defining new types, as well as objects that belong to them. Traits in Fortress exist in
889	a multiple inheritance hierarchy rooted at the traits \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.
890	\revision{revival-index}{The Working Draft of February 2011 rooted the
891	hierarchy at \TYP{Object}; \TYP{Index}, which the revival adds to the
892	library, extends only \TYP{Any} (\secref{trait-decls}).}
893	A trait declaration includes a set of method declarations,
894	some of which may be abstract.
895	For example, here is a declaration of a simple trait named \TYP{Moving}:
896	
897	\label{movingDim}
898	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Moving.tex}
899	
900	The set of traits extended by trait \TYP{Moving} are listed in braces after
901	\KWD{extends}. Trait \TYP{Moving} inherits all
902	methods declared by each trait it extends.
903	The two methods \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity} declared in trait \TYP{Moving}
904	are \emph{abstract}; they contain no body.
905	Their return types are vectors of length 3, whose elements are
906	of type \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
907	As in mathematical notation,
908	a vector of length $n$ with element type $T$ is written
909	\EXP{T^{n}}.
910	
911	Traits can also declare concrete methods,
912	as in the following example:
913	
914	\label{fastDim}
915	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Fast.tex}
916	
917	Trait \TYP{Fast} extends a single trait, \TYP{Moving}. (Because it extends
918	only one trait, we can elide the braces in its \KWD{extends} clause.)
919	It inherits both abstract methods defined in \TYP{Moving}, and it provides
920	a concrete body for method \VAR{velocity}.
921	
922	Trait declarations can be extended by other trait declarations,
923	as well as by \emph{object declarations}.
924	There are two kinds of object declarations:
925	\emph{singleton declarations} and
926	\emph{constructor declarations}.
927	
928	A singleton declaration declares a sole, stand-alone, \emph{singleton object}.
929	For example:
930	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Sol.tex}
931	
932	The object \TYP{Sol} extends two traits: \TYP{Moving} and \TYP{Stellar},
933	and provides definitions for the abstract methods it inherits. Objects must
934	provide concrete definitions for all abstract methods they inherit. \TYP{Sol}
935	also defines a field \VAR{spectralClass}.
936	For every field included in an object
937	definition, an implicit getter is defined for that field. Calls to
938	the getter of the field of an object consist of an expression
939	denoting the object
940	followed by a dot and the name of the field. For example, here is a call to the
941	getter \VAR{spectralClass} of object \TYP{Sol}:
942	
943	
944	
945	%Sol.spectralClass
946	\begin{Fortress}
947	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass}\)
948	\end{Fortress}
949	
950	If a field includes modifier \KWD{settable},
951	an implicit setter is defined for the
952	field. Calls to setters look like assignments.
953	Here is an assignment to field \VAR{spectralClass}
954	of object \TYP{Sol}:
955	
956	%Sol.spectralClass := G3
957	\begin{Fortress}
958	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass} \ASSIGN G_{3}\)
959	\end{Fortress}
960	
961	In fact,
962	all accesses to a field from outside the object to which the field belongs
963	must go through the getter of the field, and all assignments to it must go
964	through the setter. (There is simply no other way
965	syntactically to refer to the field.)
966	
967	If a field includes modifier \KWD{hidden}, no implicit getter is defined for the object.
968	
969	
970	The self parameter of a method can be given a position other than the default
971	position. For example, here is a definition of a type where the
972	self parameters appear in nonstandard positions:
973	
974	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.List.tex}
975	
976	In both methods \VAR{cons} and \VAR{append}, the self parameter occurs as the second parameter.
977	Calls to these methods look more like function calls than method calls. For example, in the following
978	call to \VAR{append}, the receiver of the call is \EXP{l_{2}}:
979	
980	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.append.tex}
981	
982	
983	A constructor declaration declares an \emph{object constructor}.
984	In contrast to singleton declarations, a constructor declaration includes
985	value parameters in its header, as in the following example:
986	\label{particleDim}
987	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Particle.tex}
988	
989	Every call to the constructor of \TYP{Particle} yields a new object.
990	For example:
991	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.p1.tex}
992	
993	The parameters to an object constructor implicitly define
994	fields of the object, along with their getters (by default). These parameters
995	can include all of the modifiers that an ordinary field can. For example,
996	a parameter can include the modifier \KWD{hidden}, in which case a getter
997	is not implicitly defined for the field.
998	
999	In the definition of \TYP{Particle}, it is the implicitly defined getters of
1000	fields \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity} that provide concrete definitions
1001	for the inherited abstract methods from trait \TYP{Moving}.
1002	
1003	In both singleton and constructor declarations,
1004	implicitly defined getters and setters can be overridden by defining
1005	explicit getters and setters,
1006	using the modifiers \KWD{getter} and \KWD{setter}. For example,
1007	we alter the definition
1008	of \TYP{Particle} to include an explicit
1009	getter for field \VAR{velocity} as follows:
1010	
1011	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1012	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)
1013	%  extends Moving
1014	%  getter velocity() = do
1015	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1016	%    velocity
1017	%  end
1018	%end
1019	\begin{Fortress}
1020	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\
1021	\(                \VAR{velocity} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3})\)\-\\\poptabs
1022	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1023	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1024	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\
1025	\(    \VAR{velocity}\)\-\\\poptabs
1026	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1027	\(\KWD{end}\)
1028	\end{Fortress}
1029	
1030	The explicitly defined getter first prints a message and then returns
1031	the value of the
1032	field \VAR{velocity}. \emph{Note that the final variable reference in this getter refers
1033	directly to the field \VAR{velocity}, not to the getter.} Only within an object definition
1034	can fields be accessed directly. In fact, even in an object definition, fields are only
1035	accessed directly when they are referred to as simple variables. In the following definition
1036	of \TYP{Particle}, the getter \VAR{velocity} is recursively accessed through the special variable
1037	\KWD{self} (bound to the receiver of the method call):
1038	
1039	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1040	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)
1041	%  extends Moving
1042	%  getter velocity() = do
1043	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1044	%    self.velocity
1045	%  end
1046	%end
1047	\begin{Fortress}
1048	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\
1049	\(                \VAR{velocity} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3})\)\-\\\poptabs
1050	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1051	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1052	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\
1053	\(    \mathord{\KWD{self}}.\VAR{velocity}\)\-\\\poptabs
1054	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1055	\(\KWD{end}\)
1056	\end{Fortress}
1057	
1058	Now, the result of a call to getter \VAR{velocity} is an infinite loop (along with a lot of output).

1060	\subsection{Traits, Getters, and Setters}
1061	Although traits do not include field declarations, they can include getter and setter declarations, as in the following
1062	alternative definition of trait \TYP{Moving}:
1063	
1064	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1065	%  getter position(): (RR Length)^3
1066	%  getter velocity(): (RR Velocity)^3
1067	%end
1068	\begin{Fortress}
1069	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1070	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{position}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1071	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1072	\(\KWD{end}\)
1073	\end{Fortress}
1074	
1075	Now, an object extending trait \TYP{Moving} must provide the definitions of
1076	\emph{getters} (as opposed to ordinary methods)
1077	for \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity}.
1078	The advantage of this definition is that we can use getter
1079	notation on a variable of static type \TYP{Moving}:
1080	
1081	% v : Moving = ...
1082	% v.position
1083	\begin{Fortress}
1084	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Moving} = \ldots\)\\
1085	\( v.\VAR{position}\)\-\\\poptabs
1086	\end{Fortress}
1087	
1088	In fact, getters can be declared in a trait definition using field declaration syntax, as in the following example
1089	(which is equivalent to the definition of \TYP{Moving} above):
1090	
1091	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1092	%  position: (RR Length)^3
1093	%  velocity: (RR Velocity)^3
1094	%end
1095	\begin{Fortress}
1096	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1097	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{position}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1098	\(  \VAR{velocity}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1099	\(\KWD{end}\)
1100	\end{Fortress}
1101	
1102	Getter declarations in trait definitions must not include bodies.
1103	A getter declaration can include the various modifiers
1104	allowed on a field declaration, with similar results.
1105	For example, if the modifier \KWD{settable} is used, then a
1106	setter is implicitly declared, in addition to a getter.
1107	
1108	\section{Features for Library Development}
1109	The language features introduced above are sufficient for the vast majority of applications programming. However, Fortress
1110	has also designed to be a good language for \emph{library} programming. In fact, much of the Fortress language as viewed
1111	by applications programmers actually consists of code defined in libraries, written in a small core language. By defining as
1112	much of the language as possible in libraries, our aim is to allow the language to evolve gracefully as new demands are placed on it.
1113	In this section, we briefly mention some of the features that make Fortress a good language for library development.
1114	
1115	\subsection{Generic Types and Static Parameters}
1116	As in other languages, Fortress allows types to be parametric with respect to other types, as well as other ``static'' parameters,
1117	including integers, booleans, dimensions, units, and operators.
1118	Fortress provides some standard parametric types,
1119	such as \TYP{Array} and \TYP{Vector}.
1120	Programmers can also define new traits, objects, and functions that include static parameters.
1121	
1122	\subsection{Specification of Locality and Data Distribution}
1123	Fortress includes a facility for expressing programmer intent concerning the distribution of large data structures
1124	at run time. This intent is expressed through special data structures called \emph{distributions}.
1125	In fact, all arrays and matrices include distributions. These distributions
1126	are defined in \library.
1127	In most cases, the default distributions
1128	will provide programmers with good performance over a variety of machines. However, in some circumstances,
1129	performance can be improved by overriding the default selection of distributions.
1130	Moreover, some programmers might wish to define new distributions, tailored for particular
1131	platforms and programs.
1132	
1133	\subsection{Operator Overloading}
1134	Operators in Fortress can be overloaded with new definitions.
1135	Here is an alternative definition of the \VAR{factorial} function, defined as a postfix operator:
1136	
1137	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.factorial.tex}
1138	
1139	As with mathematical notation, Fortress allows operators to be defined as prefix, postfix,
1140	and infix. More exotic operators can even be defined as subscripting (i.e., applications of the
1141	operators look like subscripts), and as bracketing (i.e., applications of the operators
1142	look like the operands have been simply enclosed in brackets).
1143	
1144	\subsection{Definition of New Syntax}
1145	Fortress provides a facility for the definition of new syntax in libraries.
1146	This facility is useful for defining libraries for domain-specific languages,
1147	such
1148	as SQL, XML, etc.
1149	It is also used to encode some of
1150	the language constructs seen by applications
1151	programmers.
