33	In this chapter, we provide a high-level overview of the entire Fortress
34	language. We present most features in this chapter through the use of examples,
35	which should be accessible to programmers of other languages.
36	In this chapter, unlike the rest of the specification,
37	no attempt is made to provide complete descriptions
38	of the various language features presented. Instead, we intend this overview to
39	provide useful context for reading other sections of this specification,
40	which provide rigorous definitions for what is merely
41	introduced here.
42	
43	\section{The Fortress Programming Environment}
44	\seclabel{programming-env}
45	
46	Although Fortress is independent of the properties of a particular
47	platform on which it is implemented, it is helpful for concreteness
48	to present the programming model used in the Fortress reference implementation.
49	In this programming model,
50	Fortress source code is stored in files and organized in
51	directories, and there is a text-based shell from which we can store
52	environment variables and issue commands to execute and compile
53	programs.
54	
55	A Fortress program can be processed in one of two ways:
56	
57	\begin{itemize}
58	
59	\item It can be \emph{executed}. The Fortress program is stored in a file with
60	the suffix ``\shellcommand{.fss}'' and executed directly from an underlying
61	operating
62	system shell by calling the command ``\shellcommand{fortress run}'' on it.
63	For example,
64	suppose we write the following \(\hbox{\rm``\STR{Hello,~world!}''}\) program
65	to a file ``\shellcommand{HelloWorld.fss}'':
66	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.shell.a.tex}
67	
68	The first line is an \emph{export statement};
69	we ignore it for the moment.
70	The second line defines a function \VAR{run},
71	which takes a parameter named \VAR{args}
72	and prints the string \(\hbox{\rm``\STR{Hello,~world!}''}\).
73	Note that the parameter \VAR{args}
74	does not include a declaration of its type.
75	In many cases,
76	 types can be elided in Fortress and inferred from context.
77	(In this case,
78	the type of \VAR{args} is inferred based on the program's export statement,
79	explained in \secref{overview:apis}.)
80	
81	We can execute this program by issuing the following command to the shell:
82	
83	\shellcommand{fortress run HelloWorld.fss}
84	
85	The instruction \shellcommand{fortress run} can be abbreviated as \shellcommand{fortress}:
86	
87	\shellcommand{fortress HelloWorld.fss}
88	
89	\item It can be \emph{compiled}. In this case, the Fortress program is
90	compiled into a
91	\emph{component}, which is stored in a hidden persistent cache maintained by the implementation,
92	called a \emph{fortress}. Typically, a single fortress holds all the components
93	of a user, or group of users sharing programs and libraries.
94	In our examples,
95	we often refer to the fortress we are storing components in
96	as \emph{the resident fortress}.
97	
98	For example, we could have written our \(\hbox{\rm``\STR{Hello,~world!}''}\)
99	program as follows:
100	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/HelloWorld.tex}
101	
102	We can compile this program, by issuing the command
103	``\shellcommand{fortress compile}'' on it:
104	
105	\shellcommand{fortress compile HelloWorld.fss}
106	
107	As a result of this command, a component named ``\TYP{HelloWorld}'' is stored
108	in the resident fortress. The name of this component is provided by
109	the enclosing component declaration surrounding the code. If there is
110	no enclosing component declaration, then the contents of the file are
111	understood to belong to a single component whose name is that of the
112	file it is stored in, minus its suffix. For example, suppose we write the
113	following program in a source file named ``\shellcommand{HelloWorld2.fss}'':
114	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/HelloWorld2.tex}
115	
116	When we compile this file:
117	
118	\shellcommand{fortress compile HelloWorld2.fss}
119	
120	the result is that a new component with the name \TYP{HelloWorld2} is stored
121	in the resident fortress.
122	Once this component is compiled,
123	we can execute it by issuing
124	the following command:
125	
126	\shellcommand{fortress run HelloWorld2.fss}
127	
128	Compiling a source file allows us to catch static errors before running a program.
129	It also allows the system to perform static optimizations on a program and use those
130	optimizations when executing.
131	
132	Once a program is compiled, the cached code will be used during execution unless
133	modifications have been made to the source file since the most recent compilation.
134	If the source file is newer, the program is recompiled before execution.
135	
136	\end{itemize}
137	
138	A source file must contain exactly one component declaration, and its name must
139	match the file name.
140	
141	In a compiled file,
142	multiple component declarations may be included.
143	For example, we could write the following file
144	\shellcommand{HelloWorld3.fss}:
145	
146	%component HelloWorld
147	%   export Executable
148	%   run(args) = print "Hello, world!"
149	%end
150	%
151	%component HelloWorld2
152	%   export Executable
153	%   run(args) = print "Hi, it's me again!"
154	%end
155	\begin{Fortress}
156	\(\KWD{component} \TYP{HelloWorld}\)\\
157	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}\)\\
158	\(   \VAR{run}(\VAR{args}) = \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{Hello,~world!}''}\)\-\\\poptabs
159	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
160	\(\KWD{component} \TYP{HelloWorld2}\)\\
161	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}\)\\
162	\(   \VAR{run}(\VAR{args}) = \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{Hi,~it's~me~again!}''}\)\-\\\poptabs
163	\(\KWD{end}\)
164	\end{Fortress}
165	
166	When we compile this file, the result is that both the components
167	\TYP{HelloWorld} and \TYP{HelloWorld2} are stored in the resident fortress.
168	
169	If a fortress already contains a component with the same name as a
170	newly installed component, the new component shadows the old one. For
171	example, if we first compile the source file \shellcommand{HelloWorld3.fss}
172	above and then compile the following file \shellcommand{HelloWorld4.fss}:
173	
174	%component HelloWorld
175	%   export Executable
176	%   run(args) = print "I didn't expect that!"
177	%end
178	\begin{Fortress}
179	\(\KWD{component} \TYP{HelloWorld}\)\\
180	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}\)\\
181	\(   \VAR{run}(\VAR{args}) = \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{I~didn't~expect~that!}''}\)\-\\\poptabs
182	\(\KWD{end}\)
183	\end{Fortress}
184	
185	then executing the component \TYP{HelloWorld} on our fortress will result in
186	printing of the following text:
187	
188	\begin{verbatim}
189	I didn't expect that!
190	\end{verbatim}
191	
192	We can also ``remove'' a component from a fortress.
193	For example:
194	
195	\shellcommand{fortress remove HelloWorld}
196	
197	After issuing this command, we can no longer refer to \shellcommand{HelloWorld}
198	component when issuing commands to the fortress.
199	(However, a removed component might still exist as a constituent of other,
200	\emph{linked}, components; see \secref{overview:apis}.)
201	
202	\label{overviewComponent}
203	\section{Exports and Imports}
204	\seclabel{overview:apis}
205	
206	When a component is defined, it can include \emph{export statements}.
207	For example,
208	all of the components we have defined thus far
209	have included the export statement ``\EXP{\KWD{export} \TYP{Executable}}''.
210	Export statements list various \emph{APIs}
211	that a component implements.
212	Unlike in other languages, APIs in
213	Fortress are themselves program constructs; programmers can rely on
214	standard APIs, and declare new ones. API declarations are sequences of
215	declarations of
216	variables, functions, and other program constructs, along with their
217	types and other
218	supporting declarations. For example, here is the definition of API
219	\TYP{Executable}:
220	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Executable.tex}
221	
222	This API contains the declaration of a single function \VAR{run},
223	whose type is \EXP{(\TYP{String}\ldots) \rightarrow ()}. This type is an
224	\emph{arrow type}; it declares the type of a function's parameter,
225	and its return type. The function \VAR{run} includes a single
226	parameter; the notion \EXP{(\TYP{String}\ldots)} indicates that it is a
227	\emph{varargs} parameter; the function \VAR{run} can be called with an
228	arbitrary number of string arguments. For example, here are
229	valid calls to this function:
230	
231	%run("a simple", " example")
232	%run("run(...)")
233	%run("Nobody", "expects", "that")
234	\begin{Fortress}
235	\(\VAR{run}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{a~simple}''},\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{~example}''})\)\\
236	\(\VAR{run}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{run(...)}''})\)\\
237	\(\VAR{run}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{Nobody}''},\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{expects}''},\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{that}''})\)
238	\end{Fortress}
239	
240	
241	The return type of \VAR{run} is \EXP{()}, pronounced ``void''.
242	Type \EXP{()} may be used in Fortress as a return type
243	for functions that have no meaningful return value.
244	There is a single value with type \EXP{()}:
245	the value \EXP{()}, also pronounced ``void''.
246	References to value \EXP{()} as opposed
247	to type \EXP{()} are resolved by context.
248	
249	As with components, APIs can be defined in files and compiled. APIs
250	must be defined in files with the suffix \shellcommand{.fsi}.
251	An \shellcommand{.fsi} file contains
252	source code for exactly one API, and its name must match the file name,
253	minus the suffix.
254	If there are  no explicit ``\KWD{api}''
255	headers, the file is understood to define a single API whose name is
256	the name of the containing file (minus its suffix).
257	
258	An API is compiled with the shell command ``\shellcommand{fortress compile}''.
259	When an API is compiled,
260	it is installed in the resident fortress.
261	
262	
263	For example, if we store
264	the following API in a file named ``\shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi}'':
265	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Zeepf.tex}
266	then we can compile this API with the following shell command:
267	
268	\shellcommand{fortress compile Zeepf.fsi}
269	
270	This command compiles the API \TYP{Zeepf}
271	and installs it in the resident fortress.
272	%If we omit the enclosing API declaration,
273	%so that the file \shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi} consists solely of the following code:
274	
275	%foo: String -> ()
276	%baz: String -> String
277	%\begin{Fortress}
278	%\(\VAR{foo}\COLON \TYP{String} \rightarrow ()\)\\
279	%\(\VAR{baz}\COLON \TYP{String} \rightarrow \TYP{String}\)
280	%\end{Fortress}
281	
282	%then the file is assumed to consist of the declaration of a single API
283	%named \TYP{Zeepf}.
284	
285	Unlike component compilation, API compilation does not shadow
286	existing elements of a fortress.
287	If we attempt to compile an API with the same name as an API
288	already defined
289	in the resident fortress, an error is signaled
290	and the fortress is left unchanged. To remove an API, we must
291	first remove all components referring to the API,
292	and then issue the shell command ``\shellcommand{fortress removeApi}''.
293	
294	
295	A component that exports an API must provide a definition
296	for every program construct declared in the API. For example, because
297	our component \TYP{HelloWorld}:
298	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/HelloWorld.tex}
299	exports the API \TYP{Executable}, it must include a definition for the
300	function \VAR{run}.
301	The definition of \VAR{run} in \TYP{HelloWorld} need not include
302	declarations of the
303	parameter type or return type of \VAR{run}, as these can be inferred
304	from the
305	definition of API \TYP{Executable}.
306	
307	Components are also allowed to \emph{import} APIs. A component that
308	imports an API is allowed to use any of the program constructs
309	declared in that API. For example, the following component imports the API
310	\TYP{Zeepf} and calls the function \VAR{foo} declared in \TYP{Zeepf}:
311	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Blargh.tex}
312	
313	The component \TYP{Blargh} imports declaration \VAR{foo} from the API \TYP{Zeepf}
314	and exports the API
315	\TYP{Executable}. Its \VAR{run} function is defined by calling function
316	\VAR{foo}, defined in \TYP{Zeepf}.
317	In an import statement of the form:
318	%import A.{S}
319	\begin{Fortress}
320	\(\KWD{import}\:A.\{S\}\)
321	\end{Fortress}
322	all names in the list of names \VAR{S} are imported from API $A$, and can be
323	referred to as unqualified names within the importing component. In
324	the example above, the names we have imported consist of a
325	single name: \VAR{foo}. If we had instead written:
326	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Blargh2.tex}
327	then we would have been able to refer to both \VAR{foo} and \VAR{baz}
328	as unqualified names in \TYP{Blargh}.
329	
330	Note that no component refers directly to another component,
331	or to constructs defined in another component.
332	Instead, \emph{all external references go through APIs}.
333	This level of indirection provides us with significant power.
334	It provides a way to hide implementation details in a component.
335	Also, our intention is that in future implementations,
336	it will be possible to make use of APIs to provide sophisticated
337	link and upgrade operations for the purposes of building
338	large programs.
339	%Programmers will be able to link together components from separate
340	%programming teams, swap in revised components into deployed
341	%applications, and even test components that rely on expensive libraries
342	%by wiring them up to special
343	%\emph{mock components} that provide just enough functionality to allow
344	%for testing.
345	
346	Components that contain no import statements and export the API
347	\TYP{Executable} are referred to as \emph{executable components}. They
348	can be compiled and executed directly as stand-alone components. All
349	of our \TYP{HelloWorld} components are executable components.
350	However,
351	if a component imports one or more APIs, it cannot be executed as a
352	stand-alone program. Instead, its imports are resolved to
353	other components that export all of the APIs it imports,
354	to form a new \emph{compound} component. For example, we define
355	the following component in a file named \shellcommand{Ralph.fss}:
356	\note{The example is commented out because it is not supported yet nor run by the interpreter.}
357	%\input{\home/library/examples/Ralph.compile.tex}
358	
359	We can now issue the following shell commands:
360	
361	\shellcommand{fortress compile Ralph.fss} \\
362	\shellcommand{fortress compile Blargh.fss} \\
363	\shellcommand{fortress run Blargh.fss} \\
364	
365	The first two commands compile files \shellcommand{Ralph.fss} and
366	\shellcommand{Blargh.fss},
367	respectively, and install them in the resident fortress. The third
368	command tells the resident fortress to run component \TYP{Blargh}.
369	References to API \TYP{Zeepf} in \TYP{Blargh} are resolved to their
370	implementation in component \TYP{Ralph}.
371	
372	All references to API \TYP{Zeepf} in \TYP{Gary} are resolved
373	to the declarations provided in \TYP{Ralph}.
374	
375	Note that forming the compound component \TYP{Gary} has no effect on the
376	components \TYP{Ralph} and \TYP{Blargh}.
377	These components remain in the resident
378	fortress, and they can be linked together with other components to
379	form yet more compound components.
380	Conversely, if \TYP{Blargh} or \TYP{Ralph} is
381	recompiled, deleted, or otherwise updated,
382	there is no effect on \TYP{Gary}.
383	Conceptually, \TYP{Gary} contains its own copies
384	of the components \TYP{Blargh} and \TYP{Ralph},
385	and these copies are not corrupted by actions on other components.
386	For this reason, we say that components in Fortress
387	are \emph{encapsulated}. (Of course, there are optimization tricks
388	that a fortress can use to maintain the illusion of encapsulation
389	without actually copying. But these tricks are beyond the scope of
390	this specification.)
391	
392	Compound components are \emph{upgradable}: They can be upgraded with
393	new components that export some of the APIs used by their
394	constituents. For example, if a new version of \TYP{Ralph} is compiled and
395	installed in the resident fortress,
396	we can manually \emph{upgrade} \TYP{Gary} with
397	the new version by performing the following shell command:
398	
399	\shellcommand{fortress upgrade NewGary from Gary with Ralph}
400	
401	This command produces a new component, named \shellcommand{NewGary},
402	resulting from an upgrade of \shellcommand{Gary} with \shellcommand{Ralph}.
403	The components referred to as \shellcommand{Gary} and \shellcommand{Ralph}
404	are unaffected. An important property of fortress components is that
405	they are \emph{stateless}; once constructed, they are never modified.
406	Even if a component is ``removed'' from a fortress, the components
407	it is a constituent of are unaffected.
408	
409	However, we can rebind \emph{the name} \shellcommand{Gary}
410	in the resident fortress to our new component with the following command:
411	
412	\shellcommand{fortress upgrade Gary from Gary with Ralph}
413	
414	or simply:
415	
416	\shellcommand{fortress upgrade Gary with Ralph}
417	
418	Now, the original component referred to by \shellcommand{Gary} is
419	shadowed; it cannot be referred to directly from the shell.
420	However, it might still exist in the fortress as a constituent of
421	other components, which are unmodified by the upgrade.
422	To upgrade all components in a fortress at once
423	with a new version of \shellcommand{Ralph} (rebinding all
424	names to the resulting upgrades), we can issue the command:
425	
426	\shellcommand{fortress upgradeAll Ralph}

428	\section{Automatic Generation of APIs}
429	\seclabel{apitool}
430	
431	Note that the component named \TYP{Zeepf} exports the API
432	\TYP{Zeepf}. Components and APIs exist in separate namespaces, and therefore
433	it is allowed for a component to have the same name as an API.
434	In fact, if we hadn't already defined and compiled API \TYP{Zeepf},
435	we could generate it automatically
436	from the definition of component \TYP{Zeepf}
437	with the following shell command:
438	
439	\shellcommand{fortress api Zeepf.fss}
440	
441	This command generates a new source file, \shellcommand{Zeepf.fsi}, in the
442	same directory as \shellcommand{Zeepf.fss}, which includes declarations for
443	all program constructs defined in \shellcommand{Zeepf.fss}.
444	
445	In general, if a component $C$ exports an API $A$ with the same name as $C$,
446	it is possible to automatically generate a source file
447	for the API $A$ from $C$
448	by issuing the shell command \shellcommand{fortress api} on the file
449	containing the definition of $C$.
450	This API contains declarations for all definitions in $C$ that are not
451	declared in other APIs exported by $C$, and that do not include
452	the modifier \KWD{private}.
453	If a source file with the name of $A$ already exists in the
454	same directory as the source file of $C$, an error is signaled,
455	and no file is created.
456	
457	If there is more than one component defined in a file,
458	APIs are generated for all components defined in the file that
459	export APIs with the same name as the respective component.
460	Each generated API is placed in a separate source file whose
461	name corresponds to the name of the API it defines.
462	
463	Note that the API corresponding to an automatically generated source
464	file is not automatically added to the resident fortress; the source
465	file must still be compiled via a separate action. Often, programmers
466	may want to edit the autogenerated file before compiling it to the
467	fortress.
468	
469	It is not always desirable for a component to export an API of the same name.
470	Many components will export only publicly defined standard APIs.
471	However, automatic generation of APIs from components may be useful,
472	particularly for components defined internally by a development team.
473	Large projects may contain many internally defined components that
474	are never released externally,
475	except as constituents of compound components.
476	
477	\section{Rendering}
478	
479	One aspect of Fortress that is quite different from many other languages
480	is that various program constructs are rendered in particular fonts,
481	so as to emulate mathematical notation.
482	For example, variable names are rendered in italic fonts.
483	Many other program constructs have their own rendering rules. For
484	example, the operator \verb$^$ indicates superscripting in
485	Fortress.
486	A function definition consisting of the following ASCII characters:
487	
488	\begin{verbatim}
489	f(x) = x^2 + sin x - cos 2 x
490	\end{verbatim}
491	
492	is rendered as follows:
493	
494	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Rendering.a.tex}
495	
496	Array indexing, written with brackets:
497	
498	\begin{verbatim}
499	a[i]
500	\end{verbatim}
501	
502	is rendered as follows:
503	
504	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Rendering.b.tex}
505	
506	There are many other examples of special rendering conventions.
507	
508	Fortress also supports the use of Unicode characters~\cite{Unicode} in
509	identifiers. In order to make it easy to enter such characters with
510	today's input devices, Fortress defines a convention for keyboard
511	entry: ASCII names (and abbreviations) of Unicode characters can be
512	written in a program in all caps (with spaces replaced by underscores).
513	Such identifiers are converted to Unicode characters. For example,
514	the identifier:
515	
516	\begin{verbatim}
517	GREEK_CAPITAL_LETTER_LAMBDA
518	\end{verbatim}
519	
520	is automatically converted into the identifier:
521	
522	$\Lambda$
523	
524	There are also ASCII abbreviations for writing down commonly used
525	Fortress characters. For example, ASCII identifiers for all Greek
526	letters are converted to Greek characters
527	(e.g., ``\txt{lambda}'' becomes $\lambda$
528	and ``\txt{LAMBDA}'' becomes $\Lambda$).

569	\section{Some Common Types in Fortress}
570	
571	Fortress provides a wide variety of standard types, including
572	\TYP{String}, \TYP{Boolean}, and various numeric types.
573	The floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (written in ASCII as \verb$RR64$)
574	is the type of 64-bit precision floating-point numbers.
575	For example, the following function takes a 64-bit
576	 float and returns a 64-bit float:

591	\subsection{Juxtaposition and function application}
592	
593	In the definition of \VAR{factorial},
594	note the juxtaposition of parameter \VAR{n} with the recursive
595	call \EXP{\VAR{factorial}(n - 1)}.
596	In Fortress, as in mathematics,
597	multiplication is represented through juxtaposition.
598	By default,
599	two expressions of numeric type that are juxtaposed
600	represent a multiplication.
601	On the other hand,
602	juxtaposition of an expression of function type
603	with another expression to its right
604	represents function application,
605	as in the following example:
606	
607	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.sin.tex}
608	
609	Moreover, juxtaposition of expressions of string type
610	represents concatenation, as in the following example:
611	
612	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Juxt.String.tex}
613	
614	In fact, juxtaposition is an operator in Fortress,
615	just like \EXP{+} and \EXP{-},
616	that is overloaded based on the runtime types of its arguments.
617	
618	There is a special case concerning juxtaposition that is important to mention:
619	When writing a numeric literal, the \emph{digit-group separator},
620	\txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE} (U+202F),
621	may be included between the digits in order to improve readability.
622	In ASCII,
623	this character can be abbreviated in the context of a numeric literal
624	(\emph{and only in this context}) with the character \txt{'}.
625	For example, the number 299,792,458 can be denoted in ASCII by the
626	following numeric literal:
627	
628	\begin{verbatim}
629	299'792'458
630	\end{verbatim}
631	
632	This literal is converted into Unicode by replacing all occurrences of
633	\txt{'} with \txt{NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE}:
634	%299 792 458
635	\begin{Fortress}
636	\(299{}\;792{}\;458\)
637	\end{Fortress}
638	This is not an application of the juxtaposition operator;
639	rather, it is a single token.
640	Note that commas cannot be used to separate digits because ambiguities
641	would arise with the use of commas in other expressions,
642	such as tuples.
643	
644	\subsection{Keyword Parameters}
645	
646	Functions in Fortress can be defined to take keyword arguments by
647	providing default values for parameters. In
648	the following example:
649	
650	%makeColor(red:ZZ64 = 0, green:ZZ64 = 0, blue:ZZ64 = 0) =
651	%   if 0 <= red <= 255 AND 0 <= green <= 255 AND 0 <= blue <= 255
652	%   then Color(red,green,blue)
653	%   else throw Error end
654	\begin{Fortress}
655	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{red}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{green}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0, \VAR{blue}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = 0) =\)\\
656	{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(   \KWD{if} 0 \leq \VAR{red} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{green} \leq 255 \wedge 0 \leq \VAR{blue} \leq 255 \)\\
657	\(   \KWD{then} \TYP{Color}(\VAR{red},\VAR{green},\VAR{blue})\)\\
658	\(   \KWD{else}\;\;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error} \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
659	\end{Fortress}
660	
661	the function \VAR{makeColor} takes three keyword arguments, all of
662	which default to \EXP{0}. If we call it as follows:
663	
664	%makeColor(green = 255)
665	\begin{Fortress}
666	\(\VAR{makeColor}(\VAR{green} = 255)\)
667	\end{Fortress}
668	
669	the arguments \VAR{red} and \VAR{blue} are both given the value \EXP{0}.
670	
671	There are some other aspects of this example worth mentioning.
672	For example,
673	the body of this function consists of an \KWD{if} expression.
674	The test of the \KWD{if} expression checks that
675	all three parameters have values between \EXP{0} and \EXP{255}. The
676	boolean operator \EXP{\leq} is \emph{chained}: An expression of
677	the form \EXP{x \leq y \leq z} is equivalent to the expression
678	\EXP{x \leq y \wedge y \leq z}, just as in mathematical notation.
679	The \KWD{then} clause provides an example of a constructor call in Fortress,
680	and the \KWD{else} clause shows us an example
681	of a \KWD{throw} expression in Fortress.
682	\note{How can we tell this from the example?
683	Indeed, in general, we can't distinguish constructors from other functions
684	looking only at the call sites.}

802	\section{Dimensions and Units}
803	
804	Numeric types in Fortress can be annotated with physical units and
805	dimensions. For example, the following function declares that its
806	parameter is a tuple represented in the units \EXP{\mathrm{kg}} and
807	\EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}},
808	respectively:
809	
810	\note{I MANUALLY EDITED THIS CODE -Victor}
811	%kineticEnergy(m:RR64 kg_, v:RR64 m_/s_):RR64 kg_ m_^2/s_^2 = (m v^2) / 2
812	\begin{Fortress}
813	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(m\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}, v\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\COLONOP\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}^{2} = (m\ v^{2}) / 2\)
814	\end{Fortress}
815	
816	A value of type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{kg}} is a
817	64-bit float representing a measurement in kilograms.
818	When the function \VAR{kineticEnergy} is called, two values in its tuple
819	argument are statically checked to ensure that they are in the right units.
820	
821	All commonly used dimensions and units are provided in \library.
822	Unit symbols are encoded with trailing underscores;
823	such identifiers are rendered in roman font.
824	For example the unit \EXP{\mathrm{m}} is represented as \verb$m_$.
825	For each unit, both longhand and shorthand names are provided
826	(e.g., \EXP{\mathrm{m}},
827	\EXP{\mathrm{meter}}, and \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}).
828	The various names of a given unit can be used interchangeably.
829	Also, some units (and dimensions) are defined to be synonymous
830	with algebraic combinations of other units (and dimensions).
831	For example, the unit \EXP{\mathrm{N}} is defined to be synonymous
832	with the unit \EXP{\mathrm{kg}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}}
833	and the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Force}} is defined to be synonymous with
834	\EXP{\mathrm{Mass}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{Acceleration}}.
835	Likewise, the dimension \EXP{\mathrm{Acceleration}}
836	is defined to be synonymous with \EXP{\mathrm{Velocity}/\mathrm{Time}}.
837	
838	Measurements in the same unit can be compared, added, subtracted,
839	multiplied and divided.
840	Measurements in different units can be multiplied and divided.
841	For example, we can write the following variable declaration:
842	
843	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5 seconds_
844	\begin{Fortress}
845	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
846	\end{Fortress}
847	
848	However, the following variable declaration is a static error:
849	
850	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 seconds_) / 5 seconds_
851	%I CREATED THE CODE BELOW MANUALLY -Victor
852	\begin{Fortress}
853	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{seconds}) / 5\,\mathrm{seconds}\)
854	\end{Fortress}
855	
856	In addition, the following variable declaration is a static error
857	because the unit of the left hand side of this declaration
858	is \EXP{\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}}
859	whereas the unit of the right hand side
860	is simply \EXP{\mathrm{m}} (or \EXP{\mathrm{meters}}):
861	
862	%v : RR m_/s_ = (3 meters_ + 4 meters_) / 5
863	\begin{Fortress}
864	\(v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} = (3\,\mathrm{meters} + 4\,\mathrm{meters}) / 5\)
865	\end{Fortress}
866	
867	It is also possible to convert a measurement in one unit to
868	a measurement of another unit of the same dimension,
869	as in the following example:
870	
871	%kineticEnergy(3.14 kg_, 32 f_/s_ in m_/s_)
872	\begin{Fortress}
873	\(\VAR{kineticEnergy}(3.14\,\mathrm{kg}, 32\,\mathrm{f}/\mathrm{s} \KWD{in} \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s})\)
874	\end{Fortress}
875	
876	The second argument to \EXP{\VAR{kineticEnergy} } is a measurement in
877	feet per second,
878	converted to meters per second.

942	\section{Comprehensions}
943	Another way in which Fortress mimics mathematical notation is in its support for
944	\emph{comprehensions}.  Comprehensions describe the elements of a collection by
945	providing a rule that holds for all of the collection's elements.  The elements
946	of the collection are computed in parallel by default.
947	For example, we define a set \VAR{s} that consists of all elements of another
948	set \VAR{t} divided by 2, as follows:
949	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.s.tex}
950	
951	The expression to the left of the vertical bar
952	explains that elements of \VAR{s} consist of every value \EXP{x/2}
953	for every valid value of \VAR{x} (determined by the right hand side).
954	The expression to the right of the vertical bar
955	explains how the elements \VAR{x} are to be \emph{generated}
956	(in this case, from the set \VAR{t}).
957	The right hand side of a comprehension can consist of multiple generators.
958	For example, the following set consists of every element
959	resulting from the sum of an element of \VAR{s} with an element of \VAR{t}:
960	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.sum.tex}
961	
962	The right hand side of a comprehension can also contain
963	\emph{filtering expressions} to constrain the elements provided by other clauses.
964	For example, we can stipulate that \VAR{v} consists of
965	all nonnegative elements of \VAR{t} as follows:
966	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.filter.tex}
967	
968	There is a comprehension expression for every form of aggregate expression.
969	For example, here is a list comprehension in Fortress:
970	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Expression.comprehension.l.tex}

972	all elements of the set \VAR{v} multiplied by \EXP{2}.

974	In the case of an array comprehension, the expression to the left of the bar
975	includes a tuple indexing the elements of the array.
976	For example, the following comprehension describes a \EXP{3 \times 3}
977	array, all of whose elements are zero.
978	%[(x,y) = 0 | x <- {0,1,2}, y <- {0,1,2}]

980	\([(x,y) = 0 \mid x \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}, y \leftarrow \{0,1,2\}]\)

1019	\label{overviewTest}
1020	\section{Tests and Properties}
1021	Fortress includes support for automated program testing.
1022	A new test in a component can be defined using the \KWD{test} modifier
1023	on a top-level function definition with type ``\EXP{()\rightarrow()}''.
1024	For example, here is a test function that calls the \VAR{factorial}
1025	function on some representative values
1026	and checks that the calls result in values greater than or equal to what was provided:
1027	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Tests.tex}
1028	
1029	%test factorialResultLarger [x <- 0:100] = x <= factorial(x)
1030	\begin{Fortress}
1031	\(\KWD{test} \VAR{factorialResultLarger} [x \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}100] = x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x)\)
1032	\end{Fortress}
1033	
1034	The values for \VAR{x} are generated from the provided range
1035	\EXP{0\COLONOP{}100}.
1036	
1037	Programs are also allowed to include \emph{property} declarations, documenting boolean conditions that a program is
1038	expected to obey. Property declarations are similar syntactically to test declarations. Unlike test declarations,
1039	property declarations do not specify explicit finite collections over which the property is expected to hold.
1040	Instead, the parameters in a property declaration are declared to have types, and the property is expected to hold
1041	over all values of those types. For example, here is a property declaring that \VAR{factorial} is greater than or equal
1042	to every argument of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}:
1043	
1044	%property factorialResultAlwaysLarger = FORALL (x : ZZ) (x <= factorial(x))
1045	\begin{Fortress}
1046	\(\KWD{property} \VAR{factorialResultAlwaysLarger} = \forall (x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\; (x \leq \VAR{factorial}(x))\)
1047	\end{Fortress}
1048	
1049	When a property declaration includes a name, the property identifier is bound to a function whose parameter and body are that of the property,
1050	and whose return type is \TYP{Boolean}.
1051	A function bound in this manner is referred to as a \emph{property function}.
1052	A property function can be called from within tests to ensure that a
1053	property holds at least for all values in some finite set of values.

1062	a multiple inheritance hierarchy rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.

1086	
1087	Trait \TYP{Fast} extends a single trait, \TYP{Moving}. (Because it extends
1088	only one trait, we can elide the braces in its \KWD{extends} clause.)
1089	It inherits both abstract methods defined in \TYP{Moving}, and it provides
1090	a concrete body for method \VAR{velocity}.
1091	
1092	Trait declarations can be extended by other trait declarations,
1093	as well as by \emph{object declarations}.
1094	There are two kinds of object declarations:
1095	\emph{singleton declarations} and
1096	\emph{constructor declarations}.
1097	
1098	A singleton declaration declares a sole, stand-alone, \emph{singleton object}.
1099	For example:
1100	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Sol.tex}
1101	
1102	The object \TYP{Sol} extends two traits: \TYP{Moving} and \TYP{Stellar},
1103	and provides definitions for the abstract methods it inherits. Objects must
1104	provide concrete definitions for all abstract methods they inherit. \TYP{Sol}
1105	also defines a field \VAR{spectralClass}.
1106	For every field included in an object
1107	definition, an implicit getter is defined for that field. Calls to
1108	the getter of the field of an object consist of an expression
1109	denoting the object
1110	followed by a dot and the name of the field. For example, here is a call to the
1111	getter \VAR{spectralClass} of object \TYP{Sol}:
1112	
1113	
1114	
1115	%Sol.spectralClass
1116	\begin{Fortress}
1117	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass}\)
1118	\end{Fortress}
1119	
1120	If a field includes modifier \KWD{settable},
1121	an implicit setter is defined for the
1122	field. Calls to setters look like assignments.
1123	Here is an assignment to field \VAR{spectralClass}
1124	of object \TYP{Sol}:
1125	
1126	%Sol.spectralClass := G3
1127	\begin{Fortress}
1128	\(\TYP{Sol}.\VAR{spectralClass} \ASSIGN G_{3}\)
1129	\end{Fortress}
1130	
1131	In fact,
1132	all accesses to a field from outside the object to which the field belongs
1133	must go through the getter of the field, and all assignments to it must go
1134	through the setter. (There is simply no other way
1135	syntactically to refer to the field.)
1136	
1137	If a field includes modifier \KWD{hidden}, no implicit getter is defined for the object.
1138	
1139	
1140	The self parameter of a method can be given a position other than the default
1141	position. For example, here is a definition of a type where the
1142	self parameters appear in nonstandard positions:
1143	
1144	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.List.tex}
1145	
1146	In both methods \VAR{cons} and \VAR{append}, the self parameter occurs as the second parameter.
1147	Calls to these methods look more like function calls than method calls. For example, in the following
1148	call to \VAR{append}, the receiver of the call is \EXP{l_{2}}:
1149	
1150	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.append.tex}
1151	
1152	
1153	A constructor declaration declares an \emph{object constructor}.
1154	In contrast to singleton declarations, a constructor declaration includes
1155	value parameters in its header, as in the following example:
1156	\label{particleDim}
1157	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.Particle.tex}
1158	
1159	Every call to the constructor of \TYP{Particle} yields a new object.
1160	For example:
1161	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.p1.tex}
1162	
1163	The parameters to an object constructor implicitly define
1164	fields of the object, along with their getters (by default). These parameters
1165	can include all of the modifiers that an ordinary field can. For example,
1166	a parameter can include the modifier \KWD{hidden}, in which case a getter
1167	is not implicitly defined for the field.
1168	
1169	In the definition of \TYP{Particle}, it is the implicitly defined getters of
1170	fields \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity} that provide concrete definitions
1171	for the inherited abstract methods from trait \TYP{Moving}.
1172	
1173	In both singleton and constructor declarations,
1174	implicitly defined getters and setters can be overridden by defining
1175	explicit getters and setters,
1176	using the modifiers \KWD{getter} and \KWD{setter}. For example,
1177	we alter the definition
1178	of \TYP{Particle} to include an explicit
1179	getter for field \VAR{velocity} as follows:
1180	
1181	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1182	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)
1183	%  extends Moving
1184	%  getter velocity() = do
1185	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1186	%    velocity
1187	%  end
1188	%end
1189	\begin{Fortress}
1190	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\
1191	\(                \VAR{velocity} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3})\)\-\\\poptabs
1192	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1193	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1194	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\
1195	\(    \VAR{velocity}\)\-\\\poptabs
1196	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1197	\(\KWD{end}\)
1198	\end{Fortress}
1199	
1200	The explicitly defined getter first prints a message and then returns
1201	the value of the
1202	field \VAR{velocity}. \emph{Note that the final variable reference in this getter refers
1203	directly to the field \VAR{velocity}, not to the getter.} Only within an object definition
1204	can fields be accessed directly. In fact, even in an object definition, fields are only
1205	accessed directly when they are referred to as simple variables. In the following definition
1206	of \TYP{Particle}, the getter \VAR{velocity} is recursively accessed through the special variable
1207	\KWD{self} (bound to the receiver of the method call):
1208	
1209	%object Particle(position : (RR Length)^3,
1210	%                velocity : (RR Velocity)^3)
1211	%  extends Moving
1212	%  getter velocity() = do
1213	%    print "velocity getter accessed"
1214	%    self.velocity
1215	%  end
1216	%end
1217	\begin{Fortress}
1218	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Particle}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{position} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3},\)\\
1219	\(                \VAR{velocity} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3})\)\-\\\poptabs
1220	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{extends} \TYP{Moving}\)\\
1221	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}() = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1222	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{print}\;\hbox{\rm``\STR{velocity~getter~accessed}''}\)\\
1223	\(    \mathord{\KWD{self}}.\VAR{velocity}\)\-\\\poptabs
1224	\(  \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
1225	\(\KWD{end}\)
1226	\end{Fortress}
1227	
1228	Now, the result of a call to getter \VAR{velocity} is an infinite loop (along with a lot of output).
1229	
1230	\subsection{Traits, Getters, and Setters}
1231	Although traits do not include field declarations, they can include getter and setter declarations, as in the following
1232	alternative definition of trait \TYP{Moving}:
1233	
1234	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1235	%  getter position(): (RR Length)^3
1236	%  getter velocity(): (RR Velocity)^3
1237	%end
1238	\begin{Fortress}
1239	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1240	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{position}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1241	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{velocity}()\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1242	\(\KWD{end}\)
1243	\end{Fortress}
1244	
1245	Now, an object extending trait \TYP{Moving} must provide the definitions of
1246	\emph{getters} (as opposed to ordinary methods)
1247	for \VAR{position} and \VAR{velocity}.
1248	The advantage of this definition is that we can use getter
1249	notation on a variable of static type \TYP{Moving}:
1250	
1251	% v : Moving = ...
1252	% v.position
1253	\begin{Fortress}
1254	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( v \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Moving} = \ldots\)\\
1255	\( v.\VAR{position}\)\-\\\poptabs
1256	\end{Fortress}
1257	
1258	In fact, getters can be declared in a trait definition using field declaration syntax, as in the following example
1259	(which is equivalent to the definition of \TYP{Moving} above):
1260	
1261	%trait Moving extends { Tangible, Object }
1262	%  position: (RR Length)^3
1263	%  velocity: (RR Velocity)^3
1264	%end
1265	\begin{Fortress}
1266	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Moving} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Tangible}, \TYP{Object}\,\}\)\\
1267	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{position}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Length})^{3}\)\\
1268	\(  \VAR{velocity}\COLON (\mathbb{R}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Velocity})^{3}\)\-\\\poptabs
1269	\(\KWD{end}\)
1270	\end{Fortress}
1271	
1272	Getter declarations in trait definitions must not include bodies.
1273	A getter declaration can include the various modifiers
1274	allowed on a field declaration, with similar results.
1275	For example, if the modifier \KWD{settable} is used, then a
1276	setter is implicitly declared, in addition to a getter.
1277	
1278	\section{Features for Library Development}
1279	The language features introduced above are sufficient for the vast majority of applications programming. However, Fortress
1280	has also designed to be a good language for \emph{library} programming. In fact, much of the Fortress language as viewed
1281	by applications programmers actually consists of code defined in libraries, written in a small core language. By defining as
1282	much of the language as possible in libraries, our aim is to allow the language to evolve gracefully as new demands are placed on it.
1283	In this section, we briefly mention some of the features that make Fortress a good language for library development.
1284	
1285	\subsection{Generic Types and Static Parameters}
1286	As in other languages, Fortress allows types to be parametric with respect to other types, as well as other ``static'' parameters,
1287	including integers, booleans, dimensions, units, and operators.
1288	Fortress provides some standard parametric types,
1289	such as \TYP{Array} and \TYP{Vector}.
1290	Programmers can also define new traits, objects, and functions that include static parameters.
1291	
1292	\subsection{Specification of Locality and Data Distribution}
1293	Fortress includes a facility for expressing programmer intent concerning the distribution of large data structures
1294	at run time. This intent is expressed through special data structures called \emph{distributions}.
1295	In fact, all arrays and matrices include distributions. These distributions
1296	are defined in \library.
1297	In most cases, the default distributions
1298	will provide programmers with good performance over a variety of machines. However, in some circumstances,
1299	performance can be improved by overriding the default selection of distributions.
1300	Moreover, some programmers might wish to define new distributions, tailored for particular
1301	platforms and programs.
1302	
1303	\subsection{Operator Overloading}
1304	Operators in Fortress can be overloaded with new definitions.
1305	Here is an alternative definition of the \VAR{factorial} function, defined as a postfix operator:
1306	
1307	\input{\home/preliminaries/examples/Overview.factorial.tex}
1308	
1309	As with mathematical notation, Fortress allows operators to be defined as prefix, postfix,
1310	and infix. More exotic operators can even be defined as subscripting (i.e., applications of the
1311	operators look like subscripts), and as bracketing (i.e., applications of the operators
1312	look like the operands have been simply enclosed in brackets).
1313	
1314	\subsection{Definition of New Syntax}
1315	Fortress provides a facility for the definition of new syntax in libraries.
1316	This facility is useful for defining libraries for domain-specific languages,
1317	such
1318	as SQL, XML, etc.
1319	It is also used to encode some of
1320	the language constructs seen by applications
1321	programmers.
1322

10	
11	# What a fortress was for
12	
13	## The answer
14	
15	- **The editions.** 1.0α (September 2006) and 1.0β (March 2007) describe the whole system, in the same words: a fortress, and the operations compile, link, execute, upgrade, extract, install, uninstall, hide and constrain. The 1.0 release (March 2008) cut all of it except compiling and running. It kept the word "fortress", but as "a hidden persistent cache maintained by the implementation".
16	- **Was it put back?** Yes. The Working Draft's sources entered git between 2009-10-20 and 2009-11-06. They carry the β text of the components chapter whole, and a chapter 2 that pastes β paragraphs back into the 1.0 text. The same commit that put chapter 2 back marked it "out of date". Four days later the preface listed "components linking" as not yet supported. The team never edited that text again.
17	- **What it corresponds to.** No single construct. The linking is closest to the units of PLT Scheme and to the functors of ML: code that names only interfaces, joined by a separate link step. The store is closest to the Nix package store: immutable installed things, and names that are rebound to new ones. The team names ML and Scheme modules itself. The other comparisons are from general knowledge.
18	- **What they were going after.** In the team's words, "the stability benefits of static linking with the sharing and upgrading benefits of dynamic linking". A program is linked once and then never changes under its user. Yet a library inside it can be replaced without the program's source, and a library's author can refuse a replacement.
19	- **Today.** The tree compiles a component, links it by rewriting names in its jar, and runs it. It has caches, not a fortress. No upgrade, no compound component, no extract or install.
20	
21	A term used throughout: a **component** is a unit of compiled code. An **api** is an interface, a list of declarations. A component *exports* the apis that it implements and *imports* the apis that it uses.
22	
23	## The life of a component, as the chapter tells it
24	
25	The example is that of 1.0α and 1.0β, section 2.1 to 2.2 (`Specification-history/fortress.1.0alpha.pdf`, pages 16 to 21). The Working Draft has the same steps except step 4, which it lost (below).
26	
27	1. **Write `HelloWorld.fss`.** It holds `component HelloWorld`, `export Executable`, and a function `run`. `Executable` is an api with one declaration, `run`. Why: a component never says what it *is* to the outside except through an api.
28	2. **`fortress compile HelloWorld.fss`.** The compiler checks the component and stores it in the fortress under the name `HelloWorld`. From here on, commands name the component, not the file. Why: the fortress, not the file system, is where compiled code lives. Compiling a second file with a component of the same name *shadows* the first: the name now means the new one.
29	3. **Write and compile an api and two more components.** `Zeepf.fsi` declares `foo` and `baz`. `Blargh.fss` imports `Zeepf` and exports `Executable`. `Ralph.fss` exports `Zeepf`. Each is compiled alone. `Blargh` cannot run: it uses `Zeepf`, and nothing yet says who implements `Zeepf`. Why: `Blargh` is compiled against the api only, so it can be compiled, shipped and tested before any implementation is chosen.
30	4. **`fortress link Gary from Ralph with Blargh`.** The fortress makes a new component, `Gary`, whose *constituents* are `Ralph` and `Blargh`. Inside `Gary`, `Blargh`'s uses of `Zeepf` mean `Ralph`. `Gary` exports `Executable` and imports nothing, so it can run. `Ralph` and `Blargh` stay as they were. Why: linking is the only place where an api is bound to an implementation. It is a command of the user, not a line of source.
31	5. **`fortress run Gary`.** The fortress calls `Gary`'s `run`.
32	6. **A new `Ralph.fss` is compiled.** The name `Ralph` now means the new component. `Gary` is not affected: "Conceptually, Gary contains its own copies of the components Blargh and Ralph". Why: a program that worked yesterday works today, whatever was installed since. This is what static linking gives.
33	7. **`fortress upgrade Gary with Ralph`.** The fortress makes a new component from `Gary`, with the new `Ralph` in the place of the old, and rebinds the name `Gary` to it. `Blargh` is not recompiled. The old `Gary` still exists wherever it is a constituent of something else. `fortress upgradeAll Ralph` does this for every component that holds a `Ralph`. Why: this is what dynamic linking gives, a library replaced under a program. But it happens when the user asks, to the programs the user names, and the old program is not destroyed.
34	8. **`fortress remove HelloWorld`.** The name is unbound. Components that hold `HelloWorld` as a constituent are not affected.
35	
36	The components chapter (chapter 22 of α and β) adds two steps that chapter 2 does not show.
37	
38	9. **`extract` and `install`.** `extract` writes a component to a file, with its apis and constituents. A list of *prerequisite* apis leaves out the constituents that implement them. `install` on another fortress reads the file and fills the prerequisites from that fortress. Why: "a prereqs argument allows a component to be serialized without having to include all of its libraries; new libraries can be provided when the component is installed at a destination fortress" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/basic.tex:434-437`).
39	10. **`hide` and `constrain`.** They make a component that no longer shows some of its apis. Why: among other reasons, so that two components that use different implementations of one api can be linked together (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/advanced.tex:15-35`).
40	
41	## The editions, side by side
42	
43	Provenance of each edition: `Specification-history/README.md`.
44	
45	**1.0α, 19 September 2006** (`Specification-history/fortress.1.0alpha.pdf`)
46	
47	- Chapter 2, sections 2.1 "The Fortress Programming Environment", 2.2 "Exports, Imports, and Linking Components" and 2.3 "Automatic Generation of APIs", pages 16 to 21. The commands: `fortress script`, `compile`, `run`, `remove`, `removeApi`, `link`, `upgrade`, `upgradeAll`, `api`.
48	- It defines the word: a program is "compiled into one or more components, which are stored in a persistent database called a fortress".
49	- Chapter 22, "Components and APIs", pages 162 to 178. Section 22.7, "Basic Fortress Operations": compile, link, execute, upgrade, extract and install, uninstall, testing. Section 22.8, "Advanced Features of Fortress Operations": constrain and hide.
50	- Chapter 39, a library api `Fortress.Components` "for use by components themselves (e.g., development environments)". Appendix C, a formal account of components and apis.
51	- The chapter says where it comes from: "The system described in this chapter is based on that described in [2]", and [2] is "E. Allen, V. Luchangco, and S. Tobin-Hochstadt. Encapsulated Upgradable Components, Mar. 2005."
52	
53	**1.0β, 6 March 2007** (`Specification-history/fortress.1.0beta.pdf`)
54	
55	- The same sections at the same numbers: 2.1 to 2.3 from page 18, chapter 22 from page 171, chapter 39, appendix C.
56	- Chapter 22's sections 22.7 and 22.8 read the same as α's. A comparison of the two texts with layout removed shows no changed sentence, only moved figures and footnote numbers.
57	- Chapter 2 differs in small points. The import example is `import foo from Zeepf` where α wrote `import {foo} from Zeepf`. Section 2.3 gains a paragraph: "Note that the API corresponding to an automatically generated source file is not automatically added to the resident fortress; the source file must still be compiled via a separate action."
58	
59	**1.0, 31 March 2008** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`)
60	
61	- Section 2.1 keeps the title and the `HelloWorld` example. The commands are `fortress run file.fss` and `fortress compile`. `remove`, `link`, `upgrade` and `upgradeAll` are gone. Section 2.2 is retitled "Exports and Imports". Section 2.3 on generated apis is gone.
62	- The changed definition (page 16): the program "is compiled into a component, which is stored in a hidden persistent cache maintained by the implementation. called a fortress". It adds: "Once a program is compiled, the cached code will be used during execution unless modifications have been made to the source file since the most recent compilation."
63	- The promise, in place of the β paragraph on linking (page 19): "our intention is that in future implementations, it will be possible to make use of APIs to provide sophisticated link and upgrade operations for the purposes of building large programs."
64	- The example ends with `fortress run Blargh.fss`, and "References to API Zeepf in Blargh are resolved to their implementation in component Ralph." No command chooses `Ralph`.
65	- Chapter 20, "Components and APIs", pages 117 to 121. It has four sections: overview, components, apis, and "Component and API Identity". The fortress operations, chapter 39's api and appendix C are gone. It still says "Linking components produces new components, whose constituents are the components that were linked together", and no longer says how.
66	- The reference to the 2005 paper stays in the bibliography.
67	
68	**The Working Draft, as the team left it on 2 February 2011** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/`)
69	
70	- The components chapter is β's chapter back, whole: `basic/components/overview.tex`, `basic.tex` (compile at line 32, link 76, execute 171, upgrade 248, extract and install 419, uninstall 558, testing 580) and `advanced.tex` (constrain 63, hide 89). The library api is back (`advanced-lib/components.tex`), and the formal appendix (`appendices/components.tex`).
71	- The team marked it. At the head of the chapter: "This chapter including various syntax is out of date." (`basic/components/intro.tex:12`). At the head of the appendix: "This chapter might not be up to date." (`appendices/components.tex:15`). In the linking text: "THERE IS ANOTHER RESTRICTION ON LINKING, but it is trivially met if you can't hide APIs." (`basic/components/basic.tex:148-150`).
72	- Chapter 2 (`preliminaries/overview.tex`) is a splice of two editions. It keeps 1.0's definition, "a hidden persistent cache" (line 91), and 1.0's promise of "future implementations" (lines 334-338), with the β sentences that the promise replaced still there as comments (lines 339-344). It restores β's `fortress remove` (line 195), `removeApi` (line 292), the whole passage on encapsulation and `fortress upgrade` (lines 372-426) and section 2.3.
73	- The splice lost one command. The restored passage speaks of the compound component `Gary` ("All references to API Zeepf in Gary are resolved", line 372), but the command that makes `Gary`, `fortress link Gary from Ralph with Blargh`, is not in the file. The example before it still ends with 1.0's `fortress run Blargh.fss` (line 363). So the draft upgrades a component that it never builds. This is why section 2.1 to 2.2 reads as breadcrumbs.
74	- Its head note says so: "From \secref{programming-env} to \secref{apitool} are out of date." (line 23), that is, sections 2.1 to 2.3.
75	
76	**Did 1.0 remove it as not implemented?** Yes. The 1.0 preface: "In order to synchronize the specification with the implementation, it was necessary both to add features to the implementation and to drop features from the specification." And: "many other minor language features defined in the Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0β have been elided. All of these features require additional research before they can be implemented reliably". The preface names static checks, syntactic abstraction, distributions and nested transactions. It does not name components or linking. The cut of linking shows only in the text, and in the "future implementations" sentence above.
77	
78	**Did 1.0 promise to put it back?** Yes, in general: "our goal in moving forward is to incrementally add back features taken out of the specification as they are implemented. In particular, all language features included in the Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0β remain goals for eventual inclusion in the language (perhaps with additional modification and evolution of their design)."
79	
80	**Did the Working Draft put it back?** Yes, as text, and not because it had been implemented. The dates, from the contents of each commit (a path's `git log` is not reliable here, `explorations/coordinator/map/design-intent-sources.md:93`):
81	
82	- The specification's sources are not in git before 2009-10-20 (`d8859d236f`, "[spec] Added chapter headings."). The LaTeX of α, β and 1.0 is not in the repository.
83	- 2009-11-02 (`cec470a34b`): the components chapter's files appear as stubs, and the formal appendix whole.
84	- 2009-11-05 (`d26c347121`, "[spec] Added the Preliminaries part."): chapter 2 appears, already with the β passages and already with the note "are out of date".
85	- 2009-11-06 (`0f49d86983`, "[spec] Added the entire spec files. The next task is to integrate the technical decisions since 1.0."): the components chapter's full text.
86	- 2009-11-09 (`61e28a78c4`, "[spec] Added a list of NYI features."): the preface's list. Its last item is "components linking" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex:95`).
87	- After that, chapter 2 and `basic/components/basic.tex` change once, on 2011-02-02, and only in the copyright header.
88	- The preface of the draft states the policy: "This specification is a working draft; it is meant to include all language features included in the Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0β ... and any language changes since then. ... it may include wild ideas that require additional research before they can be implemented reliably." (`preamble.tex:42-49`).
89	
90	So the fortress operations were in α and β, out of 1.0, and back in the draft in November 2009 as β's unrevised text, marked out of date on the day it came back.
91	
92	## What they were going after, in their words
93	
94	All line numbers are of `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. The same sentences are in α and β, chapter 22.
95	
96	- **The aim in one sentence.** "Fortress programs are developed, compiled, and deployed as encapsulated upgradable components that exist not only as programming language features, but also as self-contained run-time entities that are managed throughout the life of the software. ... With components and APIs, Fortress provides the stability benefits of static linking with the sharing and upgrading benefits of dynamic linking." (`basic/components/intro.tex:165-176`)
97	- **Why code names only apis.** "A key design choice we make is to require that components never refer to other components directly; all external references are to APIs. This requirement allows programmers to extend and test existing components more easily, swapping new implementations of libraries in and out of programs at will." (`basic/components/overview.tex:26-31`). And in α and β, section 2.2: "Programmers are able to link together components from separate programming teams, swap in revised components into deployed applications, and even test components that rely on expensive libraries by wiring them up to special mock components that provide just enough functionality to allow for testing."
98	- **Why it is more than a module system.** "Components are similar to modules in other programming languages, such as those of ML and Scheme. But, unlike modules in those languages, components are designed for use during both development and deployment of software." (`overview.tex:39-42`)
99	- **Why an upgrade makes a new component.** "A key aspect of Fortress components is that they are encapsulated, so that upgrading one component does not affect any other component, even those produced by linking with the component that was upgraded. Abstractly, each component has its own copy of its constituents. However, implementations are expected to share common constituents when possible." (`overview.tex:48-53`). And: "Recall that in our system, unlike with dynamic linking, components are encapsulated so that an upgrade to one component does not affect any other component on the system. We can imagine that all operations on components copy the components that they operate on rather than share them. Because components are immutable, these two interpretations are semantically indistinguishable." (`basic.tex:401-410`)
100	- **What the fortress is.** "Users do not manipulate components directly. Instead, every component is installed in a persistent database on the system. We think of this database, which we call a fortress, as the agent that actually performs operations such as compilation, linking, upgrading, and execution of components: a virtual machine, a compiler, and a library registry all rolled into one. ... Components and APIs are immutable objects. A fortress maps names to components installed on the system. The fortress operations are modeled as methods of the fortress that change the mapping." (`overview.tex:55-70`)
101	- **What they left to the implementer.** "The ways in which fortresses are actually realized on particular platforms are beyond the scope of this specification. An implementor might choose to instantiate a fortress as a process, or as a persistent object database stored in a file system, with fortress operations being implemented as scripts that manipulate this database." (`overview.tex:73-78`)
102	- **Who controls an upgrade.** A component can be upgraded only if it exports the api `Upgradable`, with a function `isValidUpgrade`. "Developers can define their own versions of this component to restrict how their components can be upgraded. For example, they can prevent upgrades with older versions of a component, or with a matching component from an untrusted vendor." (`basic.tex:309-312`)
103	- **Shipping without the libraries, and control of access.** The prerequisites of `extract` (quoted in step 9), and: "This difference provides a means for controlling access to the extracted component, for security, legal, or other reasons." (`basic.tex:513-515`)
104	- **Hiding, and optimization across components.** The plain system "exposes to everyone all the APIs used in the development of a project", and "By allowing access to these APIs, it inhibits significant cross-component optimization." Hiding an api closes it, so that nothing outside can replace its implementation (`advanced.tex:15-45`). This is the only place where the text ties the design to optimization. It does not say what a fortress would then optimize.
105	- **Several implementations side by side.** A fortress keeps, for each api, "a list of components that implements it, in order of preference" (`basic.tex:485-487`), and installs a new component at the head of the list of each api it exports (`basic.tex:536-538`).
106	
107	Outside the specification:
108	
109	- **The team's paper** is cited and not held. "Encapsulated Upgradable Components", Eric Allen, Victor Luchangco and Sam Tobin-Hochstadt, March 2005, Sun Microsystems, number 2005-0156 (`Specification/fortress/fortress.bib:12-19`). No copy is in `Papers/`, `research/` or `research/decks/`, and the territory map has no row for components. I could not confirm that it was ever published outside Sun.
110	- **Steele, 2016.** His JuliaCon talk lists under growability "modular libraries (components and APIs, separate compilation, multiple co-existing implementations of one interface)" (our extract, `research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:49-50`). This is the extract's summary of slide 11, not a quotation of it.
111	- **The closing post, July 2012.** It lists "components and APIs" among eight aspects that the team was pleased with (`research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md:119-123`). It does not speak of fortresses or of upgrading.
112	- The 2012 restart of the specification, `Documentation/Specification/`, has no chapter on components and no sentence on fortresses or upgrades.
113	
114	## The peers
115	
116	Only the first comparison is the team's. The rest is from general knowledge, not from this repository.
117	
118	- **ML signatures, structures and functors.** The team's own comparison (`overview.tex:39-42`). Same: an api is a signature, a component is a structure, and a component with imports is a functor, code that is closed only when it is given implementations of its imports. Differs: ML's linking is an expression in the source, and ML has no store, no upgrade and nothing at deployment.
119	- **Units of PLT Scheme (Racket), and Jiazzi for Java.** Same: a unit names only signatures that it imports and exports, and a separate step links units into a *compound unit*, which is itself a unit. This is the link operation of Fortress almost word for word. Differs: units are values of a running program. They have no persistent store and no upgrade.
120	- **The Nix package store.** Same: everything installed is immutable, an "upgrade" builds a new thing beside the old, and a name (a profile) is rebound to it, so the old one still works for whatever holds it. Differs: a Nix package depends on exact other packages, not on interfaces, and no type check says that a replacement fits.
121	- **OSGi bundles.** Same: a bundle declares the packages that it imports and exports, never the bundle that supplies them, and a framework that keeps running installs, resolves and updates bundles. This is the fortress as "agent". Differs: an OSGi update changes the bundle in place for every user of it, which is the effect that Fortress's encapsulation was designed to prevent.
122	- **Java modules (since Java 9).** Same: explicit exports, and a link tool (`jlink`) that makes a closed image. Differs: `requires` names a module, not an interface. Only the service mechanism (`uses` and `provides`) binds by interface.
123	- **Swift module interfaces and library evolution.** Same: a client is compiled against a textual interface, and the library's binary can be replaced without recompiling the client. Differs: the client names the module, one implementation has that name, and the replacement is in place, for every client at once.
124	- **Static and dynamic linking in C.** The team's own frame. Static linking gives each program its own copy, which never changes and never gets a fix. Dynamic linking shares one copy, which changes under every program at once. Fortress wanted the copy to be private in meaning, shared in storage, and replaced only by a command.
125	
126	The closest for the language part is units: a component is a unit, and `link` builds a compound unit. The closest for the fortress itself is the Nix store. No peer known to me joins the two with a typed check of each replacement.
127	
128	## What is built today, and what is not
129	
130	The record: FACTS F-22, F-282 and F-294; ledger rows 320 and 841; `explorations/reviews/preface-list-provenance-2026-11-16.md`, "Components linking".
131	
132	Built:
133	
134	- **Apis and components as source.** `import` and `export`, and separate checking of a component against apis only. The compiled path checks a component against the apis that it exports (F-282, F-294). Walk does not (row 841).
135	- **`fortress compile`.** It writes one jar for each component into `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:405`).
136	- **`fortress link X` and `fortress build X`.** They compile `X` and the components behind the apis that it imports, then rewrite the api names inside the jars to component names (`Shell.java:412-421`, `linker/Linker.java:213-269`). The result is not a new named component: the jar of `X` is replaced in the cache. The linker is the team's, of January and February 2012 (`8267d2d088`, "Experimental prototype for a component system"; `1d4e967aac`), later than the draft's text.
137	- **A table of who implements what.** `linker/LinkShell.java`, reached by `bin/comp/tlink`, keeps two maps in `caches/global.map`: api to component, and (component, api) to component. Its commands are `alink`, `clink`, `arm`, `crm`, `alias`, `print`, `reset`. This is the nearest thing in the tree to the fortress's table of preferred implementations. Without an entry, an api is looked for only under its own name, so an api implemented by a component of another name is not found (F-22, row 320).
138	- **`fortress run X`.** It starts a JVM on the cache's jars (`bin/fortress:16`, `bin/run`). It takes a component's name, as the chapter's `run` does.
139	- **`fortress api X.fss`.** It writes an api from a component, as section 2.3 says (`Shell.java:427`).
140	- **Caches.** They are keyed by source path and reused while the source is unchanged. This is what the 1.0 release called a fortress.
141	
142	Not built, on either path:
143	
144	- A fortress: a store that maps names to immutable components, with shadowing and rebinding.
145	- A compound component: `link` with a result name and constituents.
146	- `upgrade`, `upgradeAll`, and the apis `Upgradable` and `Installable`.
147	- `remove` (`uninstall`), `removeApi`.
148	- `extract`, `install`, `installAPI`, and the list of preferred implementations as the chapter states it.
149	- `hide` and `constrain`.
150	- The library api `Fortress.Components`.
151	
152	`bin/fortress upgrade Gary` and `bin/fortress extract Gary` print the usage message (run on 2026-11-16 at `6c31470f6b`). `Shell.java:405-489` names none of these commands.
153	
154	The ledger holds no row for the missing operations. A row ready to file, checked with `ledger.py check --rows` (it fails only the number rule), for the section "3. Traits, objects and components":
155	
156	    | ? | the fortress operations of the components chapter other than compile, link, run and api exist on neither path: `upgrade`, `upgradeAll`, `remove`, `removeApi`, `extract`, `install`, `uninstall`, `hide` and `constrain` are no commands of `bin/fortress`, and no class builds a compound component | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (tools) | `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/basic.tex:248`, "Basic Fortress Operations"; `basic/components/advanced.tex`, "Advanced Features of Fortress Operations" | none | fortresses intent note | siblings: 320. `Shell.java:405-489` names no such command; `bin/fortress upgrade Gary` and `bin/fortress extract Gary` print the usage message ('Usage:', then ' parse [-out file] ...'). `fortress link` takes one component and rewrites api names to component names in its jar (`linker/Linker.java:213-269`); it makes no new named component. `Upgradable`, `Installable` and `Fortress.Components` are in no library. The preface lists 'components linking' as not yet supported (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex:95`). Detail: `explorations/reviews/fortresses-intent-2026-11-16.md`. |
157	
158	A second defect is in the text, not the code: the Working Draft's chapter 2 upgrades the component `Gary` and never links it (above). The revision's chapter has the same gap: `Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex` holds no `link Gary` either.
159	
160	## Can the vision be finished from what the team left?
161	
162	What the team's sources describe well enough to build from:
163	
164	- The operations and their types: compile, link, execute, upgrade, extract, install, uninstall, hide, constrain (`basic.tex`, `advanced.tex`).
165	- The conditions under which a link or an upgrade is valid, with their reasons (`basic.tex:344-398`, `advanced.tex:183-246`).
166	- The set-level model of components, apis, imports, exports and constituents (`appendices/components.tex`).
167	- The api by which a program handles components itself (`advanced-lib/components.tex`).
168	
169	What no source of the team in this repository describes:
170	
171	- **What a fortress is on disk.** The text leaves it out on purpose: "beyond the scope of this specification".
172	- **How constituents are shared.** "Implementations are expected to share common constituents when possible", and the "optimization tricks ... are beyond the scope".
173	- **How an upgrade reaches compiled code.** The text predates the compiler. It does not say whether an upgrade relinks jars, regenerates code, or only rebinds names. The 2012 linker rewrites names in a jar, in place, which is the opposite of an immutable component.
174	- **What happens to a running program.** Every operation is on stored components. Nothing speaks of replacing code in a process that is running.
175	- **How multiple dispatch crosses a link.** A function overloaded in two components must dispatch as one. The component text is of 2005 and does not treat it. The 1.0 chapter has a section "Cross-Component Overloading" (20.2.3), which is about source, not about linking.
176	- **Versions.** The text gives `isValidUpgrade` as the hook, and gives no scheme of version numbers or compatibility.
177	- **What a hidden api lets the compiler do.** The claim on cross-component optimization has no account behind it.
178	- **The 2005 paper itself**, which the chapter says it is based on, and which may answer some of the points above. To get it: Sun Labs technical reports of 2005, or the authors.
179	- **Where the team stood at the end.** The chapter's own note says "out of date" and cites a proposal of 2009 for compound apis. The team's last word on linking is the 2012 prototype, which implements a table from api to component and nothing of upgrading.
180	
181	Decisions not taken. Each is the curator's; this note recommends none.
182	
183	- Whether the revival's goal includes the fortress operations at all. The sources: β's text (2007), cut from 1.0 (2008), restored unrevised and marked out of date (2009), listed as not supported (2009), and a prototype of another shape (2012). The model program needs none of it. Doing nothing keeps today's behaviour.
184	- If it does, whether the text of 2007 or the linker of 2012 is the starting point. They disagree on whether linking makes a new component or changes one in place.
185	- Whether chapter 2 of the revision keeps the spliced text with its note, restores the lost `link` command from β, or goes back to the 1.0 wording. Only the first keeps the current text.
186	- Whether the row above is filed.

<project name="FortressSpec" default="spec">
  <description>
    The Fortress specification, written in LaTeX.
  </description>

  <property environment="env"/>
  <property name="fortress.home"
            value="${env.FORTRESS_HOME}"/>
  <property name="compiler.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/ProjectFortress"/>
  <property name="example.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/SpecData/examples"/>
  <property name="preliminaries.example.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/SpecData/examples/preliminaries"/>
  <property name="basic.example.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/SpecData/examples/basic"/>
  <property name="advanced.example.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/SpecData/examples/advanced"/>
  <property name="library.example.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/SpecData/examples/library"/>
  <property name="library.api.home"
            value="${fortress.home}/Library"/>
  <property name="library.builtin.home"
            value="${compiler.home}/LibraryBuiltin"/>
  <property name="preliminaries.ex" value="${basedir}/../preliminaries/examples"/>
  <property name="basic.ex"         value="${basedir}/../basic/examples"/>
  <property name="advanced.ex"      value="${basedir}/../advanced/examples"/>
  <property name="library.ex"       value="${basedir}/../library/examples"/>
  <property name="library.api"      value="${basedir}/../library/apis"/>
  <property name="texinputs"        value=".:${fortress.home}/Fortify:"/>
  <property name="compiler.classpath"
            value="${compiler.home}/build:${compiler.home}/third_party/xtc/xtc.jar:${compiler.home}/third_party/jsr166y/jsr166y.jar:${compiler.home}/third_party/plt/plt.jar:${compiler.home}/third_party/junit/junit.jar"/>

  <taskdef name="fortress"
           classname="com.sun.fortress.ant_tasks.FortressTask"
	   classpath="${compiler.classpath}"/>

  <taskdef name="fortex"
           classname="com.sun.fortress.ant_tasks.FortexTask"
           classpath="${compiler.classpath}"/>

  <taskdef name="foreg"
           classname="com.sun.fortress.ant_tasks.ForegTask"
           classpath="${compiler.classpath}"/>

  <target name="spec" depends="genSource, makeExs, bib">
    <exec executable="pdflatex" failonerror="true">
      <arg value="fortress"/>
      <env key="TEXINPUTS" value="${texinputs}" />
    </exec>
    <exec executable="pdflatex" failonerror="true">
      <arg value="fortress"/>
      <env key="TEXINPUTS" value="${texinputs}" />
    </exec>
  </target>

  <target name="tex" depends="makeReservedWordsFiles, bib">
    <exec executable="pdflatex" failonerror="true">
      <arg value="fortress"/>
      <env key="TEXINPUTS" value="${texinputs}" />
    </exec>
    <exec executable="pdflatex" failonerror="true">
      <arg value="fortress"/>
      <env key="TEXINPUTS" value="${texinputs}" />
    </exec>
  </target>
